content: Simple, scriptable health checks for a server. You describe checks in YAML, cron (or a systemd timer) runs onecheck, and onecheck tells you what is broken: by exit code, on stdout (text or JSON), in per-rule result files, and through an event queue that records every pass → fail and fail → pass change. How it works - Modules collect, onecheck decides. A check type (file, http, command, disk, systemd, cpu, memory, docker, ports, ...) is a separate executable, onecheck-<name , living in a modules directory. A module only returns values (status code, file size, stdout, ...). All comparisons are done by one engine inside onecheck, so every operator works the same for every module. - Modules are picked up dynamically. onecheck looks into the modules directory on every run. Install a module and the next run can use it. - State is tracked for you. For every rule onecheck remembers the confirmed state and how many runs in a row passed or failed. With fail after: 3 a rule must fail three times in a row before it is considered failed. Each confirmed change is written as a JSON event for a notification service to pick up. Quick start Getting started walks through installation, the first config and scheduling with cron or systemd. Documentation | | | |---|---| | Getting started | install, first config, cron and systemd | | Configuration | every config key, includes, defaults | | Checks | the check block: paths, all operators, JSON and JSON Schema | | Modules | file, http, command, disk, systemd, cpu, memory, docker, ports | | State and events | fail after / pass after, the event queue contract | | Output and results | exit codes, text and JSON output, result files | | Module management | search, install, update, remove, self-update | | Logging and logrotate | log files, levels, rotation, event cleanup | | Module protocol | write your own module, in any language | | Development | build, test, release | onecheck --help and onecheck <command --help describe every command and flag. The source is on GitHub.
description: Simple, scriptable health checks for a server.
title: onecheck

content: Checks The check block of a rule says what must be true about the values a module returned. It is evaluated by onecheck itself, by one engine, so everything on this page works the same for every module: bundled or third-party. A rule passes when every condition holds. Each condition that does not hold is reported separately, with what was expected and what was found: A rule without check passes whenever its module could collect the data. Paths Each key of check is a path to a value. The first part is a field of the module (see the module's page for its fields); further parts go into objects and arrays: | Path | Meaning | |---|---| | status | the field status | | headers.content-type | key content-type of the object field headers | | items.0 | first element of an array | | items.# | number of elements of an array | Paths use GJSON path syntax. A key that itself contains a dot is written with a backslash: headers.x\.y. A field that does not exist for the module is a config error, caught by onecheck validate. Conditions A condition is one of: - a plain value — shorthand for equals: - a mapping of operators — all of them must hold: - a combinator — all, any, not, described below. To compare with an object, use equals explicitly, because a bare mapping is read as operators. Operators | Operator | Applies to | Holds when | |---|---|---| | equals / not equals | anything | the value is (not) exactly this | | contains / not contains | string, array, object | substring / element / key is (not) present | | starts with / ends with | string | the string starts / ends with this | | matches / not matches | string | the regular expression matches (does not match) | | glob / not glob | string | the whole string matches (does not match) a shell pattern | | gt, gte, lt, lte | number | greater / greater-or-equal / less / less-or-equal | | in / not in | anything | the value is (not) one of the list | | exists | anything | the path is present (true) or absent (false) | | type | anything | the value has this JSON type | | length | string, array, object | a nested condition holds for the length | | every / some | array | a nested condition holds for each / at least one element | | path | anything | the other operators apply to a value inside this one | | json | string | the string is JSON and satisfies assert / schema | An operator applied to a value of the wrong type (for example gt on a string) does not hold, and the message says which type was found. An unknown operator or a malformed argument is a config error. equals, not equals Exact comparison of JSON values. There is no conversion between types: the number 200 is not equal to the string "200". contains, not contains starts with, ends with matches, not matches Regular expressions in Go RE2 syntax. The expression may match anywhere in the string; anchor it with ^ and $ for a full match. Command output usually ends with a newline, and $ only matches at the very end of the text. Use the multi-line flag (?m) to let ^ and $ match at line boundaries: Write regular expressions in single quotes so YAML leaves backslashes alone. glob, not glob Shell patterns, matched against the whole string, case-sensitive: | Pattern | Matches | |---|---| | | any run of characters, including / and none at all | | ? | exactly one character | | [abc], [a-z] | one character from the set or range | | [!abc] | one character not in the set | Everything else is literal: . is a dot, + is a plus. Quote patterns that start with or `: YAML reads those characters specially. gt, gte, lt, lte Numeric comparison. Fields that hold a size or a time span accept literals with units. The module's page marks such fields as bytes or duration : Unit literals work for equals, not equals, in, not in too, and only directly on such a field (not on values inside JSON). in, not in exists Whether the path is present at all. Use it for optional keys and for the absence of something: exists is the only operator that can hold for an absent path; see [Missing values. The file module also has a field named exists (does the file exist). check: { exists: true } compares that field; it is the plain-value shorthand, not this operator. type One of string, number, bool, object, array, null. length Applies a nested condition to the length of a string (in characters), an array (elements) or an object (keys). A plain number means equals. every, some Apply a condition to the elements of an array. The argument is a condition; a list of conditions means all of them. | | holds when | empty array | |---|---|---| | every | the condition holds for each element | holds | | some | the condition holds for at least one element | does not hold | A value that is not an array, or a missing path, does not hold. every reports each failing element separately, with its index in the path. For an element that is an object the message also shows its simple keys (strings, numbers, booleans; nested objects such as labels are left out), so you see which element it was: The index counts elements of the array the condition is applied to; after a query such as #(state=="running")# that is the filtered array. some reports one failure with the whole array. Combine with a GJSON query to pick elements first, for example only running containers: A query that matches nothing gives an empty array: every holds, some does not. path Inside any condition mapping, path moves the other operators of that mapping to a value inside the current one. It is how conditions reach the fields of array elements: path uses the same GJSON syntax as check keys and needs at least one operator next to it. A missing sub-path is handled like any missing value. Unit literals (10MB, 1h) do not apply under path: compare with plain numbers. json Parses a string field as JSON and checks the document. It works on any string field: an HTTP body, a command's stdout, a file's content. A string that is not valid JSON does not hold. At least one of assert and schema is required; both may be used together. json.assert A list of assertions. Each has a path into the parsed document and any of the operators above (several operators on one line are ANDed): Paths are GJSON paths: | Path | Selects | |---|---| | a.b.c | nested keys | | items.0 | array element by index | | items.# | number of elements | | items.#.name | the name of every element, as an array | | items.#(state=="ok") | first element whose state is ok | | items.#(state=="ok")# | all such elements, as an array | | items.#(size 100)#.name | names of all elements with size over 100 | json.schema A JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) written in YAML. Use it when the shape of the document matters: required keys, types, enumerations, formats of nested objects. Every schema violation becomes its own failure, with the location inside the document: assert is shorter for "this key has this value"; schema is better for structure. They combine freely. Combining conditions Operators written side by side are ANDed. For other logic use combinators; they nest to any depth. When any does not hold, one failure is reported for the whole any. Missing values A path can be absent: an optional header, a key that is not in the JSON, a field the module does not return in this situation (the file module returns no size for a file that does not exist). For an absent path every operator fails , including the negative ones (not equals, not contains, not matches, not in) and not: {...}. The only exceptions are exists: false and a not around exists. The message says got nothing (path is missing). The reason: missing data must never make a check pass by accident. If an API stops returning the key you are watching, the check fails instead of going quiet. When absence is acceptable, say so explicitly: An explicit JSON null is a present value: exists: true holds, and so does type: "null". Large values A module returns at most run.max field size (default 10MB) per field. When a condition uses a field that had to be cut, the rule ends with the status error rather than passing or failing on partial data. Raise the limit, or check something smaller (a file's size instead of its content`). Recipes
title: Checks

content: Configuration The config is YAML. Unknown keys are errors, so a typo never goes unnoticed. Check a config without running it: onecheck validate -c <file . Full reference Every key except name is optional; the values above are the defaults for root. Sizes accept B, KB, MB, GB, TB (1024-based); durations accept ms, s, m, h, d, w and combinations such as 1h30m. name The name is required and keeps configs on the same host apart: - results: <paths.results /<name /<rule .json - state and run lock: <paths.state /<name / - log: <log.dir /<name /onecheck.log Rule names only have to be unique within one config. The event queue (paths.events) is shared by all configs; every event carries the config name. Two different config files must not use the same name: onecheck remembers which file owns a name and refuses to run the second one (exit code 2). If you move or rename a config file and keep its name, delete <paths.state /<name /.owner once; the next run records the new location. Default paths | | root | other users | |---|---|---| | log.dir | /var/log/onecheck | $HOME/.local/state/onecheck/log | | paths.modules | /usr/lib/onecheck/modules | $HOME/.local/lib/onecheck/modules | | paths.results | /var/lib/onecheck/results | $HOME/.local/state/onecheck/results | | paths.events | /var/lib/onecheck/events | $HOME/.local/state/onecheck/events | | paths.state | /var/lib/onecheck/state | $HOME/.local/state/onecheck/state | Relative paths in the config are resolved against the directory of the config file. onecheck creates these directories with mode 0750 and the files in them (results, state, events, logs) with mode 0640. Results and events can contain pieces of what was checked, such as file content or command output, so they are not readable by everyone. To let another service read results or events, put its user into the group owning the directories. Where everything is: onecheck paths onecheck paths prints the full path of everything onecheck reads and writes for the config it would use, so the paths do not have to be worked out from the tables above: | Line | Meaning | |---|---| | config | the config file and how it was found: --config, ONECHECK CONFIG or default location | | name | the config's name; it is part of the log, state and results paths | | include | every include file that was read, in reading order | | log | the log file, see Logging and logrotate | | state | the confirmed state of each rule, see State and events | | results | the latest result of each rule | | events | the event queue, shared by all configs on the host | | modules | where modules are looked for | | binary | the onecheck executable itself, with symlinks resolved | (missing) marks a path that does not exist yet. The log, state, results and events paths are created by the first run, so they are missing on a fresh install. The command changes nothing, does not need the modules to be installed and works with rules that are broken. If the config file is found but cannot be loaded, its path is still printed, followed by the error, and the exit code is 2. onecheck paths --json prints the same for scripts: Includes (conf.d/) - Patterns are globs; relative ones are resolved against the config file's directory. A pattern that matches nothing is fine. - Files are read in lexicographic order, after the rules of the main file. - An include file may contain only the rules key: - A rule name used twice, in any files, is an error naming both files. Environment variables in params Strings inside params may reference environment variables as ${VAR}, which keeps secrets out of the config file: - Only the ${VAR} form is expanded. A plain $VAR is left alone, so shell commands in the command module keep working. - Write $${VAR} to get a literal ${VAR}. Every other $ (including the shell's $$, $1, $(...)) is passed through unchanged. - An undefined variable makes that rule an error; it is never replaced by an empty string. - check is never expanded. Logging level The level comes from, in order: --log-level, log.level, info. Two kinds of config errors Errors of the whole config stop onecheck with exit code 2 before any check runs: unreadable or invalid YAML, an unknown top-level key, a missing or invalid name, a rule without a name, a duplicate rule name, an include file with keys other than rules. Errors of a single rule make only that rule unusable. On onecheck run the rule gets the status error with the reason, and every other rule still runs. This covers: an unknown key in the rule, an invalid rule name, a missing module, a module that is not installed or not compatible, params the module does not accept, a condition on a field the module does not have, an unknown operator or a bad operator argument, an undefined ${VAR}. Such an error counts as a failure for the rule's state, so after fail after runs it produces a fail event: a broken rule is reported through the same channel as a broken service, instead of silently disappearing. onecheck validate prints all errors of both kinds and exits with 2 if there are any.
