content: Development Rules for contributors (commit messages, merges, limits) are in AGENTS.md. This page is about how to build, test and release. Requirements - Go (the version in go.mod or newer) - make - network access the first time make lint runs: it installs a pinned golangci-lint into ./bin - for the documentation site only: Node.js 22 and npm Make targets | Target | What it does | |---|---| | make build | builds dist/onecheck and dist/modules/onecheck-{file,http,command,disk,systemd,cpu,memory,docker,ports} | | make test | go test -race ./... | | make fmt | formats the code with gofmt | | make lint | golangci-lint, including cyclomatic complexity | | make check | fmt-check + go vet + lint + test; must pass before a change is done | | make release-assets | cross-builds release assets and checksums.txt into dist/release/ | | make docs-build | checks documentation links and builds the site into docs/dist/ | | make docs | builds the site and publishes it to branch docs | | make clean | removes dist/ | Builds are static (CGO ENABLED=0). The version is injected with make build VERSION=1.2.3; without it the version is dev. A new bundled module is picked up by the Makefile automatically: every directory cmd/onecheck-<name is built as a module. Cyclomatic complexity gocyclo runs as part of make lint with a limit of 25 per function (.golangci.yml). It applies to tests too. When a function goes over the limit, split it; do not raise the limit and do not silence the linter. Layout How a run flows through the packages: Design rules - Modules collect, the core decides. Never put comparison logic into a module. A new way of comparing is a new operator in internal/match, where it immediately works for all modules. - One failing rule never stops the others. Anything wrong with a single rule becomes that rule's error result. Only problems of the whole config or of onecheck's own files end a run with exit code 2. - No lost transitions. For each rule the event is written before the state. Keep that order. - Atomic files. Everything under results, state and events is written with store.WriteFileAtomic. - The protocol is a contract. Changing the JSON exchanged with modules incompatibly requires a new module.ProtocolVersion and a range in internal/modules that still accepts the old one. Tests - Unit tests sit next to the code. The matching engine and the state machine are table-driven. - Tests that need real modules build them once per package through internal/testmods (runner, cli). internal/modules uses a fake module from testdata/fakemod that can misbehave on purpose. - Module management is tested against an in-memory GitHub client (internal/install) and against a local HTTP server speaking the GitHub API shape (internal/github, internal/cli). - examples/config.yaml (with its conf.d/ includes) is loaded and validated against all bundled modules by TestExamplesLoadAndValidate, so examples cannot drift from the code. The test also fails when a bundled module (cmd/onecheck-<name ) has no example rule: a new module comes with an example. - Tests must not use the network and must not write outside t.TempDir(). Run one package or one test: Adding an operator 1. Add a table-driven case (passing and failing) to internal/match/match test.go, and a case to TestCompileErrors for bad arguments. 2. Implement it in internal/match/ops.go and register it in leafOps. 3. Document it in docs/checks.md. Adding a bundled module 1. Create cmd/onecheck-<name / with main.go (description, params schema, fields) and collect.go, following the existing modules. 2. Test collect directly; include TestDescriptionCoversFields. 3. Add docs/modules/<name .md (with title and sidebar.label frontmatter like the other module pages), list it in docs/modules/meta.ts and link it from README.md and docs/index.md. Releasing Releases are built by GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/release.yml) when a tag vX.Y.Z is pushed: The workflow runs make check, then make release-assets VERSION=1.2.0 and publishes a GitHub release with: for linux and darwin on amd64 and arm64. These names are what onecheck module install and onecheck self-update look for. After the release is published, the workflow's docs job runs make docs, which publishes the documentation of the tagged commit (see Documentation site). Environment overrides useful when testing update flows against a fork: | Variable | Effect | |---|---| | ONECHECK GITHUB API | API base URL instead of https://api.github.com | | ONECHECK SELF UPDATE REPO | repository self-update downloads from | | ONECHECK SELF UPDATE TARGET | path of the binary self-update replaces | Documentation site The pages under docs/ are published at by Blume. docs/ is the Blume project and its own content root: | Path | What it is | |---|---| | docs/blume.config.ts | site settings: base /onecheck, excluded folders | | docs/package.json, docs/package-lock.json | the pinned Blume version | | docs/index.md | the home page | | docs/meta.ts, docs/modules/meta.ts | sidebar order | | docs/public/ | static files served at the site root | Every .md page under docs/ is published, except docs/superpowers/ (internal designs and plans) and build folders. To keep a new folder off the site, add it to content.exclude in docs/blume.config.ts. Links between pages use site routes, never .md paths: Checks, disk. Blume prefixes the base /onecheck itself; it does not rewrite relative .md links, so they would break on the site. scripts/docs-check-links.sh fails the build when one appears. Links from outside the site (README, CLI messages) use the full URL https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/<route . Preview locally with cd docs && npm ci && npm run dev. make docs-build runs the link check, blume doctor and blume build; CI runs it on every push and pull request (.github/workflows/check.yml). make docs (scripts/publish-docs.sh) builds the site and commits docs/dist to branch docs, creating it on first use. GitHub Pages serves branch docs, path /. The release workflow runs it for every tag, so the site always shows the latest release.
title: Development

content: Getting started Install onecheck is one static binary plus one executable per check module. With the install script The script detects the system and CPU, asks GitHub for the latest release, verifies the download against the release's checksums.txt, and installs onecheck together with the bundled modules (file, http, command, disk, systemd, cpu, memory, docker, ports) of the same version. A specific version: Every version gets its own directory, and a symlink in a bin directory points at the chosen one: | | Linux | macOS | |---|---|---| | versions | /usr/local/lib/onecheck/versions/<version /onecheck | /.local/share/onecheck/versions/<version /onecheck | | symlink | /usr/local/bin/onecheck | /.local/bin/onecheck | | modules | /usr/lib/onecheck/modules | /.local/lib/onecheck/modules | On Linux the install is system-wide, and the script calls sudo when it is not run as root. On macOS everything stays in the home directory; if /.local/bin is not in PATH, the script says how to add it. | Option | Description | |---|---| | --version <v | version to install (0.1.0 or v0.1.0); default: the latest release. Also ONECHECK VERSION | | --root <dir | where versions are kept | | --bin-dir <dir | where the onecheck symlink is created | | --modules-dir <dir | where the bundled modules go | | --no-modules | install onecheck only | Set GITHUB TOKEN if GitHub's rate limit gets in the way. To upgrade, downgrade or switch back, run the script again. A version that is already on disk is not downloaded again, only the symlink is switched, and the modules are brought to the same version. Old versions are kept until you delete their directories under versions/. onecheck self-update refuses to touch a binary installed this way, because it would overwrite one version's directory with another version. The modules directories above are the defaults of paths.modules: the Linux one for root, the macOS one for a regular user. If you run onecheck on Linux as a regular user, set paths.modules: /usr/lib/onecheck/modules in the config, or install with --modules-dir /.local/lib/onecheck/modules. By hand 1. Download onecheck <os <arch from the releases, verify it against checksums.txt, and put it into PATH as onecheck: 2. Install the bundled modules (file, http, command, disk, systemd, cpu, memory, docker, ports): Once a config exists, --modules-dir is not needed: the directory is taken from paths.modules. Or build everything from source: make build puts the binary into dist/onecheck and the modules into dist/modules/. First config onecheck looks for its config in this order: 1. --config <path (-c) 2. $ONECHECK CONFIG 3. /etc/onecheck/config.yaml 4. $HOME/.config/onecheck/config.yaml A minimal config needs a name and some rules: Each rule has three parts: - module — which module collects the data; - params — the module's input (what to look at); - check — conditions on the values the module returns. See examples/config.yaml for a fuller example, Configuration for every key and Checks for everything check can express. Validate and run The exit code is 0 when every rule passed, 1 when something failed, 2 when onecheck could not run at all. Details: Output and results. Schedule it onecheck has no scheduler of its own. Run it from cron: or from a systemd timer: Checks at different intervals Use one config per interval, each with its own name, and one schedule line per config: Configs with different names never block each other: results, state, logs and the run lock are kept per name. If a run of the same config is still in progress when the next one starts, the new one exits with code 2. What gets written where With the default paths, for root: | What | Where | |---|---| | latest result of each rule | /var/lib/onecheck/results/<name /<rule .json | | state between runs | /var/lib/onecheck/state/<name / | | events (pass ↔ fail changes) | /var/lib/onecheck/events/ | | log | /var/log/onecheck/<name /onecheck.log | | modules | /usr/lib/onecheck/modules/ | For other users everything lives under $HOME/.local/state/onecheck/ and $HOME/.local/lib/onecheck/modules/. All of it is configurable: Configuration.
title: Getting started

content: Logging and logrotate Log file Every run appends to by default /var/log/onecheck/<name /onecheck.log for root and $HOME/.local/state/onecheck/log/<name /onecheck.log for other users. The directory is created when needed. onecheck paths prints the exact path for the current config. | Level | What is logged | |---|---| | error | a run that could not complete | | warn | recoverable problems, e.g. an unreadable state file | | info | one line per rule with its outcome, state changes, a summary per run | | debug | additionally, per rule: the params and fields requested from the module, the values it returned (long strings cut to 256 bytes), the state counters; the modules found; what modules printed on their stderr | The level is taken from --log-level, then log.level, then info: text format: json format writes the same records as one JSON object per line. Messages at warn and above are also printed on stderr, so cron mails them. With --log-level on the command line, stderr shows everything at that level as well, so a run can be watched in the terminal: log.level in the config changes only the log file, never stderr. Log lines never go to stdout, which carries only results. At debug the log contains rule params and returned values as they are, including HTTP headers and command output. Do not leave log.level: debug on if those hold secrets. If the log file cannot be opened, onecheck prints a warning, logs to stderr for that run, and still runs the checks. onecheck logrotate onecheck does not depend on the system's logrotate. One command takes care of both things that would otherwise grow forever: the log and the event queue. Schedule it, for example once a day: With several configs, run it once per config (logs are per config): Logs When onecheck.log is larger than max size: - onecheck.log becomes onecheck.log.1 (or onecheck.log.1.gz); - existing onecheck.log.N move to N+1; - the next run starts a new onecheck.log. On every call, rotated files with an index above keep, or older than max age, are removed. The log is only rotated when it is too large, so calling logrotate often is harmless. Rotation takes the config's run lock. If a run is in progress at that moment the logs are skipped with a message and handled by the next call. Events An event is written with expires at = time of the event + events.ttl. onecheck logrotate removes events whose expires at has passed. This only matters for events nobody consumed: a notification service normally deletes events as it processes them (see State and events). The event queue is shared by all configs, so the cleanup of any one config covers all of them. Each event keeps the lifetime it was written with. Files in the queue directory that cannot be read as events, and temporary files left by an interrupted write, are removed once they are older than events.ttl.
title: Logging and logrotate

content: Module management A module is an executable file named onecheck-<name in the modules directory (paths.modules). onecheck reads that directory on every run: there is no registry to refresh and nothing to restart. A module is usable from the moment its file is there, and gone when the file is removed. Modules are distributed through GitHub Releases. The onecheck module commands download, verify and install them; you can also copy a module file into the directory by hand. All commands take the modules directory from the config. Without a config, pass --modules-dir <dir . List SOURCE is the repository a module was installed from; - means the file was put there by hand. COMPATIBLE says whether this onecheck can talk to the module, see Compatibility. Search Lists every release of the repositories and the modules each release has for this machine's OS and architecture, with the command to install each. Install "Latest" is the newest release that is not marked as a pre-release. A pre-release is only installed when asked for by version. What install does, per module: 1. downloads the asset into a temporary file inside the modules directory; 2. compares its sha256 with the release's checksums.txt — a release without checksums.txt, or without an entry for the asset, is refused; 3. runs the downloaded file with describe and checks that it is the module it claims to be and speaks a supported protocol version; 4. renames it into place in one step, replacing a previous version; 5. records repository, version and checksum in installed.json in the modules directory. If any step fails, nothing changes: a previously installed version keeps working, and no partial file is left. Update Each module is updated to the latest stable release of the repository it was installed from. For every module onecheck prints either updated <name to <version or skipped <name : <reason . Reasons include: already up to date; the new release speaks a protocol this onecheck does not support (update onecheck first); the module was copied in by hand, so its source is unknown. A skip is not a failure. An update that was attempted and failed (download error, checksum mismatch, a module that does not run) stops the command with exit code 2; the installed version stays in place. Remove Rules that still use the module will get status error ("module is not installed"). Updating onecheck itself The asset onecheck <os <arch is downloaded next to the running binary, verified against checksums.txt, started once (version) to prove it runs, and then renamed over the current binary in one step. On any failure the current binary is left untouched. The user running the command needs write access to the directory of the binary. A onecheck installed with install.sh lives in a per-version directory and is not updated by self-update (the command refuses): run install.sh again, see Getting started. self-update does not touch modules, and module update does not touch onecheck. A typical sequence: Compatibility onecheck and modules are versioned independently. What must match is the module protocol : the JSON a module and onecheck exchange. - Every module reports the protocol version it speaks. - Every onecheck supports a range of protocol versions; onecheck version prints it. - A module outside that range is shown as not compatible by module list and validate; rules using it get status error; install and update refuse to install such a version. Module versions themselves (semver, the release tag without the leading v) are only used to decide whether an update is available. Bundled modules (file, http, command, disk, systemd, cpu, memory, docker, ports) are released together with onecheck from the same repository and carry the same version number, but any mix that shares a protocol version works. Repositories of third-party modules Any GitHub repository can distribute modules. A release needs: - one asset per module and platform, named onecheck-<name <os <arch , e.g. onecheck-postgres linux amd64 (<os and <arch as in Go: linux, darwin; amd64, arm64); - an asset checksums.txt in sha256sum format covering them: Module names are lower-case letters, digits, and -. See Module protocol for how to write a module. Add repositories you use to the config so that module search covers them: Environment | Variable | Effect | |---|---| | GITHUB TOKEN | sent to the GitHub API: higher rate limits, access to private repositories | | ONECHECK GITHUB API | API base URL instead of https://api.github.com (GitHub Enterprise) | Security notes - Checksums come from the same release as the files. They protect against corrupted or truncated downloads, not against a compromised repository. Only install modules from repositories you trust: a module runs with the privileges of onecheck. - Modules are looked up only in the modules directory, never in PATH. Keep that directory writable by root (or the onecheck user) only.
title: Module management

content: Module protocol This page is for people writing a module. A module teaches onecheck a new kind of check: Postgres, Redis, DNS, a message queue, anything. The idea A module is a standalone executable named onecheck-<name . onecheck starts it once per check, hands it the rule's params on stdin as JSON, and reads field values from its stdout as JSON. A module never decides whether a check passed. It returns facts ("status is 503", "the file is 2 KB"); onecheck evaluates the rule's check conditions on them. That is why every operator, JSON assertions and JSON Schema work for every module without the module doing anything. A module can be written in any language. For Go there is a small SDK, github.com/alekzonder/onecheck/pkg/module. Protocol version described here: 1 . Invocations A module must implement two subcommands. onecheck-<name describe Prints a JSON description on stdout and exits with 0. It must be fast and free of side effects: onecheck calls it on every run and on install. | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | protocol | yes | protocol version the module speaks | | name | yes | module name; must equal <name in the file name | | version | yes | module version (semver) | | description | no | one line, shown by onecheck module list | | params schema | no | JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for the rule's params; onecheck validates params with it before starting a check | | fields | yes | every field the module can return: name → type, description, and optionally "output": true | Field types: | Type | JSON value | Notes | |---|---|---| | string, number, bool, object, array | the JSON type | | | bytes | number of bytes | conditions may use 10MB etc. | | duration | number of seconds, may be fractional | conditions may use 500ms, 1h etc. | A field with "output": true is diagnostic output, like a command's stdout or a response body. onecheck asks for such fields on every check (they are added to fields of the request) and saves their tail in the result even if no condition uses them, see Output and results. Mark only what helps to understand a failure and is not expensive to collect. Declaring fields lets onecheck validate reject a condition on a field that does not exist. Use "additionalProperties": false in params schema so that typos in params are caught. onecheck-<name check Reads one request from stdin, prints one response on stdout. Request: | Key | Description | |---|---| | protocol | protocol version onecheck is using for this call | | rule | rule name, for the module's own log messages | | params | the rule's params, already validated against params schema | | fields | the fields the rule's conditions use, plus the module's output fields unless the rule has output tail: 0. A module may skip collecting everything else, which matters for expensive fields. Empty when the rule has no conditions: then collect only what is cheap | | max field size | largest size in bytes of one string value; do not read more than max field size + 1 bytes of anything | | timeout ms | the rule's timeout; finish before it | Response: | Key | Description | |---|---| | fields | field name → value. Omit a field that has no value in this situation | | truncated | names of string fields that were cut to max field size. onecheck refuses to evaluate conditions on them | | error | null, or {"message": "..."} when the data could not be collected. fields may still carry output fields collected before the failure (what a command printed before its timeout); onecheck saves them and evaluates nothing | Rules of behaviour Errors versus values. Return error when you could not find out: connection refused, permission denied, timeout. Return a value when you found out, even if the answer is bad: an HTTP 500 is status: 500, a missing file is exists: false, a non-zero exit code is exit code: 3. An error makes the rule's status error; values are judged by the user's conditions. Exit code. Exit with 0 whenever you produced a response, including one with error set. A non-zero exit code, invalid JSON on stdout, or no output means the module itself is broken; the rule gets status error. stdout is for the response only. Write diagnostics to stderr. onecheck puts a module's stderr into its log at level debug. Timeouts. onecheck starts a module in its own process group and kills the whole group a short moment after timeout ms, and also when onecheck itself is interrupted. Leave child processes in that group (do not call setsid/setpgid for them), so they are cleaned up with the module. Prefer to stop on your own before that and return an error saying what timed out. Size limits. Never read an unbounded amount into memory. Read at most max field size + 1 bytes; if there was more, cut the value to max field size and list the field in truncated. No state, no side effects. A module is started fresh for every check and may run in parallel with other checks, including other instances of itself. Environment. A module inherits onecheck's environment and runs with its privileges. Writing a module in Go The SDK implements the protocol; you provide a description and one function. What the SDK does for you: - module.Main handles describe and check, fills in protocol, applies timeout ms to the context passed to Collect, turns a returned error into the error response, and cuts over-long string values while recording them in truncated. - module.DecodeParams decodes params strictly (unknown keys are errors). - req.Wants("field") tells whether a rule uses a field; req.WantsOr("field", cheap) additionally answers cheap when the rule has no conditions at all. Use them to skip expensive work. Writing a module in another language Anything that can read stdin and print JSON works. A complete module in shell: Trying a module by hand Distributing a module Publish a GitHub release with assets named onecheck-<name <os <arch and a checksums.txt; then anyone can onecheck module install <owner/repo . Details: Module management. Protocol versions The protocol version is a single integer. It changes only when the JSON exchanged above changes incompatibly. onecheck supports a range of versions (onecheck version prints it) and passes the module's own version back in each request. Adding optional keys to requests or responses does not change the version: modules must ignore request keys they do not know, and onecheck ignores response keys it does not know.
title: Module protocol

content: Runs a command and returns its exit code and output. Params Exactly one of run and argv is required. | Key | Description | |---|---| | run | a command line, executed with sh -c; pipes, redirects and variables work | | argv | a list: program and its arguments, executed directly, without a shell | | env | extra environment variables, a mapping of name to value | | cwd | working directory | | stdin | text passed to the command on standard input | The command inherits onecheck's environment plus env. It is killed, together with everything it started, when the rule's timeout expires. Prefer argv when arguments come from elsewhere: nothing is interpreted by a shell. In run, shell variables such as $HOME, $1, $$ and $(...) reach the shell untouched; only the ${VAR} form is expanded by onecheck from its own environment first (write $${VAR} to pass it to the shell literally). Fields | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | exit code | number | exit code of the command; -1 if it was killed by a signal | | stdout | string | standard output | | stderr | string | standard error | | duration | duration | how long the command ran | A non-zero exit code is a value, not an error: check it with exit code. The rule ends with status error when the command could not be run at all (program not found, not executable, bad cwd) or hit the timeout. Note that a rule does not require exit code 0 unless you say so. Add exit code: 0 to check. The tail of stdout and stderr (the last 10k of each by default) is saved in the rule's result on every run, also when no condition mentions them and when the command hit the timeout, so a failure can be investigated afterwards. Change the size with output tail, see Output and results. stdout and stderr are each limited by run.max field size (default 10MB). Output usually ends with a newline. With equals include it ("active\n"); with matches use (?m) so $ matches before it: '(?m)^active$'. Examples
title: command module

content: Reports how busy the host's CPUs are, the load average and the number of cores, so a host that is overloaded for a long time is noticed before its services slow down. Works on Linux and macOS. Params | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | window | no | how long CPU usage is measured: 500ms, 5s, 1m, or a bare number of seconds; default 1s; from 100ms to 5m | CPU usage is the difference of two readings of the CPU counters: the module reads them, waits window, and reads them again. Write the window quoted or not: window: 5s, window: 5. The window must be shorter than the rule's timeout (default 30s); otherwise the rule is an error at once, without waiting, telling you to shorten the window or raise timeout. A longer window smooths short bursts; for sustained load combine a short window with fail after (see State and events). The module waits only when a percent field is checked. A rule that checks only load average answers immediately. Fields Usage over the window, in percent of all cores together (a 4-core host with one core fully busy shows 25), two decimals: | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | usage percent | number | busy time: everything except idle and iowait (steal counts as busy) | | user percent | number | programs (user and nice time) | | system percent | number | kernel (system, irq and softirq time) | | iowait percent | number | idle while waiting for disk; Linux only | | steal percent | number | time a virtual machine waited for the hypervisor; Linux only | Without waiting: | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | cores | number | logical CPUs | | load1, load5, load15 | number | load average over 1, 5 and 15 minutes | | load1 per core, load5 per core, load15 per core | number | load average divided by cores | Which field to use - CPU busy: usage percent. It includes steal time, so on a virtual machine a high usage percent with a high steal percent means the hypervisor is short of CPU, not your programs; check user percent/system percent for what your programs use. - Load: prefer per core to load : the same threshold then fits hosts with any number of cores. Load above 1 per core means work is waiting for a CPU. load5/load15 react slower and ignore short spikes. - On Linux load average also counts processes waiting for disk, so high load with low usage percent and high iowait percent points to slow storage rather than to the CPU. Which fields are present: - iowait percent and steal percent are missing on macOS, which does not report these times; a condition on them fails with "got nothing (path is missing)". - percent fields are missing when no rule condition asks for them. On macOS a rule that checks only iowait percent/steal percent does not wait the window. Inside a container the module reports the host's CPUs and load, not the container's limits. Reading the counters failing is an error, not a fail. Examples A failure names the rule and the value:
title: cpu module

content: Reports free space and inodes of one filesystem, so a disk that is filling up is noticed before services on it start to fail. Running out of inodes (many small files: sessions, caches, mail queues) breaks writes just like running out of space, so check both. Params | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | path | yes | a mount point, any path inside a filesystem, or a device | - A mount point (/var) or any path inside a filesystem (/var/lib/postgresql): the filesystem holding that path is reported. Symlinks are followed. - A device under /dev/ (/dev/sda1, /dev/mapper/vg-data, /dev/disk/by-uuid/...): its mount point is looked up in the mount table. Symlinks are resolved on both sides, so any name of the device works. A root filesystem listed in the mount table under a name that does not exist on disk (/dev/root on some systems) cannot be found by device; use its mount point, /, instead. One rule checks one filesystem; write one rule per disk. Checking all disks automatically is not supported yet. Fields | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | total | bytes | size of the filesystem | | free | bytes | space available to ordinary users, like df "Avail" | | used | bytes | used space: total minus all free blocks | | used percent | number | used / (used + free) 100, like df "Use%" | | inodes total | number | inodes of the filesystem | | inodes free | number | free inodes | | inodes used | number | used inodes | | inodes used percent | number | inodes used / inodes total 100 | | mountpoint | string | where the filesystem is mounted | | device | string | the mounted device, as in the mount table | | fstype | string | filesystem type, e.g. ext4, xfs, apfs | Percentages have two decimals (89.1); df rounds them up (90%). Blocks reserved for root (5 % on ext4 by default) count as unavailable, as in df: used percent reaches 100 when ordinary users can no longer write, even though root still can. bytes fields accept unit literals in conditions: free: { gt: 5GB }. See Checks. Which fields are present: - inodes are missing on filesystems without a fixed number of inodes (btrfs and some others report 0). A condition on them then fails with "got nothing (path is missing)"; leave inode conditions out for such disks. ZFS reports an inode count that grows and shrinks with free space, so inodes used percent on ZFS mostly repeats used percent. - mountpoint, device and fstype are missing if the mount table cannot be read; the numbers are still reported. A path that does not exist, a device that is not mounted, or a filesystem that cannot be queried is an error, not a fail. A rule without check passes whenever the numbers could be read, as with any module, so always give thresholds. Examples A failure names the rule and the value:
title: disk module

content: Reports Docker containers, so you know that the containers which must serve are running and healthy, that nothing restarts in a loop or dies of running out of memory, and that no unknown container is running on the host. Works on Linux and macOS with Docker, Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima, rootless Docker and Podman (its Docker-compatible API). The module always returns the same fields: the list of containers that match the params, and their number. Params only narrow the list. Params | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | name | no | container name, exact (nginx) or a shell pattern (app- ), without the leading / | | label | no | key (the label is set) or key=value, e.g. com.docker.compose.project=shop | | host | no | where Docker is: unix:///path/to/docker.sock or tcp://host:port; found automatically when omitted | Without name and label every container is listed, running or not (like docker ps -a). With both, a container must match both. A filter that matches nothing gives count: 0, not an error. Patterns use the glob syntax: , ?, [abc], [!abc]. Where Docker is When host is not set, the module takes the first of: 1. the DOCKER HOST environment variable; 2. the current Docker context (DOCKER CONTEXT, else docker context use saved in /.docker/config.json; DOCKER CONFIG moves /.docker). The default context means "no context"; 3. the first socket that exists: - /var/run/docker.sock - $XDG RUNTIME DIR/docker.sock (rootless Docker) - macOS: /.docker/run/docker.sock (Docker Desktop), /.orbstack/run/docker.sock, /.colima/default/docker.sock - $XDG RUNTIME DIR/podman/podman.sock, /run/podman/podman.sock When onecheck runs from cron or a systemd timer, its environment usually has no DOCKER HOST and maybe no HOME: set host in the rule if Docker is not at one of the default sockets. Only unix:// and tcp:// (plain HTTP) addresses are supported. A tcp:// address without a port uses 2375. TLS (DOCKER TLS VERIFY, a context with TLS certificates) and ssh:// are not supported and give an error. Every error names the address and where it came from: Reading the Docker socket is equivalent to root access on the host; give onecheck that access knowingly. Fields | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | containers | array | matching containers sorted by name | | count | number | number of matching containers | Each element of containers has all of these keys: | Key | Type | Value | |---|---|---| | name | string | container name, without the leading / | | id | string | short id (12 characters) | | image | string | image the container was created from, as written in docker run or compose: nginx:1.27, registry.local/app:3 | | state | string | created, running, paused, restarting, removing, exited, dead | | health | string | healthy, unhealthy, starting; none when the container has no healthcheck | | restart count | number | restarts done by the restart policy (restart: always, ...) | | exit code | number | exit code of the last run; 0 while it runs | | oom killed | bool | the last run was killed for running out of memory | | uptime seconds | number | seconds since the container started, while it is running or restarting; otherwise 0 | | labels | object | container labels | Element keys are checked with paths (containers.0.state) or with every / some and path. Unit literals do not work inside elements: write uptime seconds: { gt: 3600 }, not 1h. A rule that only checks count makes one request to Docker. A rule that checks containers asks Docker about each matching container too. Recipes A container must run count: 1 first: without it a missing container would only show as a missing path. No unknown containers Every running container must be allowed by its name, a name pattern or an image pattern. Allowing does not require: a container that is not running is not reported here (check required ones with the rule above). Drop #(state=="running")# to require that stopped containers are known as well. A whole compose project Crash loops and OOM kills restart count grows for the life of the container and is reset when it is recreated (a new deploy), so pick a limit above what a normal deploy cycle reaches. Image of a container Output The index (.2, .1) is the position in the (filtered) list; the element's keys in the message (all but labels) tell which container it is.
title: docker module

content: Inspects one path: a file, a directory or a symlink. Params | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | path | yes | the path to inspect | Glob patterns are not supported: one rule looks at one path. Fields | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | exists | bool | whether the path exists | | type | string | file, dir, symlink or other (socket, device, ...) | | size | bytes | file size; for a directory the total size of all files below it | | age | duration | time since the last modification | | mode | string | permission bits as four octal digits, e.g. "0640" | | owner | string | owner user name (the numeric id if it has no name) | | group | string | owner group name (the numeric id if it has no name) | | content | string | content of a regular file | | count | number | number of entries directly in a directory | | target | string | where a symlink points, exactly as stored in the link | bytes and duration fields accept unit literals in conditions: size: { lt: 10MB }, age: { lt: 1h }. See Checks. Which fields are present: | The path is | Fields returned | |---|---| | missing | exists: false only | | a regular file | everything except count and target | | a directory | everything except content and target | | a symlink to something that exists | type: symlink, target, and all other fields describing what the link points to | | a dangling symlink | exists: false, type: symlink, target | A condition on a field that is not returned fails with "path is missing", so size: { gt: 0 } on a missing file fails as it should. Only the fields a rule uses are collected. In particular content is read, and a directory's total size is computed, only when check mentions them. content is limited by run.max field size (default 10MB). A condition on a larger file ends the rule with status error; check size or raise the limit. A path that cannot be inspected at all (permission denied on a parent directory, unreadable file when content is requested) is an error, not a fail. Examples
title: file module

content: Makes one HTTP or HTTPS request. Params | Key | Required | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | url | yes | | http:// or https:// URL | | method | no | GET | HTTP method | | headers | no | | request headers, a mapping of name to value | | body | no | | request body | | follow redirects | no | true | follow redirects; with false the redirect response itself is returned | | insecure skip verify | no | false | do not verify the server's TLS certificate | The request is limited by the rule's timeout. Proxy settings are taken from the usual HTTP PROXY / HTTPS PROXY / NO PROXY environment variables. Secrets can be passed through the environment, see Configuration: Fields | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | status | number | HTTP status code | | headers | object | response headers; names in lower case , repeated headers joined with , | | body | string | response body | | duration | duration | time from sending the request until the whole body was read | | tls expires in | duration | time until the server certificate expires; https only | duration fields accept unit literals: duration: { lt: 500ms }, tls expires in: { gt: 14d }. Address a single header as headers.<name , always in lower case: headers.content-type. A response with any status code is a successful collection: 404 and 500 are values of status to be checked. The rule ends with status error, not fail, when no response could be obtained: DNS failure, connection refused, TLS handshake or certificate error, timeout. body is limited by run.max field size (default 10MB); a condition on a larger body ends the rule with status error. The tail of body (the last 10k by default) and the headers are saved in the rule's result on every run, also when no condition mentions them, so a failed status: 200 can be investigated afterwards. Change the size with output tail, or set output tail: 0 for responses that hold secrets, see Output and results. tls expires in is absent for plain http:// URLs, so a condition on it fails there. Examples
title: http module

content: Reports physical memory and swap usage of the host, so memory running out is noticed before the system starts swapping heavily or killing processes. Works on Linux and macOS. Params None. params may be omitted. Fields | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | total | bytes | physical memory | | available | bytes | memory that can be given to programs without swapping | | used | bytes | total minus available | | used percent | number | used / total 100 | | swap total | bytes | swap size | | swap used | bytes | swap in use | | swap free | bytes | free swap | | swap used percent | number | swap used / swap total 100; 0 when there is no swap | Percentages have two decimals. On Linux available is the kernel's MemAvailable: page cache and other memory the kernel can reclaim at once are not counted in used, as in the "available" column of free. A host with a large file cache therefore shows low used percent even though little memory is "free"; that is normal. On macOS available is free plus inactive memory. used then still includes active file cache and compressed and wired memory, so it reads higher than "Memory Used" in Activity Monitor, often 75–90 % on an idle Mac. On Macs prefer a threshold on available (available: { gt: 2GB }) or a higher used percent limit. macOS has no fixed swap: it adds swap files as needed, so swap total grows and shrinks, and a high swap used percent there is less alarming than on Linux. bytes fields accept unit literals in conditions: available: { gt: 1GB }. See Checks. Inside a container the module reports the host's memory, not the container's limit. Reading memory or swap failing is an error, not a fail. Examples A failure names the rule and the value:
title: memory module

content: Reports the TCP and UDP ports the host listens on, so you know that nothing unexpected is exposed and that every port which must serve is open. Linux only: the data comes from the kernel (/proc/net), the same that ss -tuln shows. No root is needed and no external command is run. A port cannot be reached from outside when nothing listens on an outside address, whatever the firewall says. Ports published by Docker are listening sockets too (of docker-proxy), so they are in the list even though Docker opens them past ufw. The module always returns the same fields: the list of listening sockets that match the params, and their number. Params only narrow the list. Params | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | proto | no | tcp or udp; both when omitted | | interface | no | only sockets bound to an address of this interface, e.g. eth0, or to all addresses | Without interface the list has every socket except those bound to a loopback address (127.0.0.0/8, ::1): what other machines could reach. With interface the list has the sockets bound to an address of that interface and the sockets bound to all addresses (0.0.0.0, ::), which answer on every interface. interface: lo lists what listens locally: the whole 127.0.0.0/8 network and ::1. An interface that does not exist is an error. interface selects by the address a socket is bound to. It is not a guarantee about packets: Linux answers on one interface for an address of another unless the firewall or rp filter forbids it. Sockets bound to a broadcast or multicast address, or to an address no interface has, are listed only without interface. Fields | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | listening | array | listening sockets sorted by proto, port, address | | count | number | number of listening sockets | Each element of listening has all of these keys: | Key | Type | Value | |---|---|---| | proto | string | tcp, udp | | port | number | port number | | address | string | 0.0.0.0 or :: for all addresses, otherwise the address the socket is bound to | | family | string | ipv4, ipv6 | | interface | string | interface that has the address; any for all addresses; "" when no interface has it | | process | string | name of the process that holds the socket; "" when onecheck may not see it | TCP sockets are those in the LISTEN state. UDP has no such state: the list has the UDP sockets without a remote address, the ones ss -uln shows. A service that opens an IPv4 and an IPv6 socket gives two elements (0.0.0.0 and ::). Many programs open only the :: socket and serve IPv4 through it: that is one element with family: ipv6, so do not use family to tell whether a port answers on IPv4. Several sockets on the same proto, address and port (worker processes) are one element and count once. process is filled for the processes onecheck may inspect: all of them as root, only its own user's otherwise. When several processes hold the socket, the one with the lowest pid is named: for a socket-activated service (ssh.socket, docker.socket) that is systemd. An address that two interfaces have is shown with the first interface by name. A rule that only checks count does not look processes up. Recipes No unknown ports Every listening socket must be an allowed one. Anything else is a failure that names the port, the address and the process. To allow a port only for one protocol or on one interface, put the conditions of one alternative into all: A port must be open listening.#.port is the list of port numbers. Write one rule per protocol, or select the protocol in the path: listening.#(proto=="udp")#.port: { contains: 51820 }. Both in one rule One interface A local service is up Limits - The firewall is not consulted. A port that listens on 0.0.0.0 and is hidden only by the firewall is in the list: allow it in the rule or bind the service to 127.0.0.1. A port that listens but is blocked by the firewall still counts as open. A firewall of the cloud provider is not visible from the host at all. - UDP is noisier than TCP. Programs open unconnected UDP sockets on random ports for a short time (DNS clients, DHCP, mosh sessions). When a "no unknown ports" rule fails now and then on UDP, check only TCP (proto: tcp) or allow the port range. - A socket bound to a device rather than an address (SO BINDTODEVICE) is shown with the address it is bound to, usually 0.0.0.0. - Port forwarding done only in the firewall (DNAT without a listening socket, Docker with userland-proxy: false) is not seen. Output
title: ports module

content: Reports the state of one systemd unit, so you know that services which must serve are running and start on boot, that units which must stay off are stopped and will not come back after a reboot, and that scheduled jobs (timers) really run and succeed. Works with any unit type: service, timer, socket, mount, path, target, ... It calls systemctl show, so it needs systemd; on other systems (macOS, Linux without systemd) every check is an error. Params | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | unit | yes | unit name, e.g. nginx.service, backup.timer, docker.socket | | user | no | true checks a unit of the user's own service manager (systemctl --user); default false | | properties | no | list of extra systemctl show property names, returned in the properties field | A name without a suffix (nginx) is understood by systemd as a service. Name exactly one unit: patterns ( , ?, [) are rejected, because systemd would report several units at once. Escaped names such as dev-disk-by\x2dlabel-root.device work as systemctl shows them. user: true is for onecheck running as an ordinary user. The user's service manager must be running: for cron or a timer outside a login session enable lingering (loginctl enable-linger <user ). If XDG RUNTIME DIR is not set, the module uses /run/user/<uid . Checking another user's units from root is not supported. One rule checks one unit; write one rule per unit. Fields All units: | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | load state | string | loaded, not-found, masked, bad-setting, error | | active state | string | active, inactive, failed, activating, deactivating, reloading | | sub state | string | type-specific state: running, exited, dead, waiting, listening, ... | | unit file state | string | enabled, disabled, static, masked, indirect, generated, ...; empty string if systemd reports none (e.g. the unit does not exist) | | result | string | result of the unit's last run: success, exit-code, signal, timeout, core-dump, ... | | description | string | unit description | | state age | duration | time since the last change of the active or sub state | Services: | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | restarts | number | automatic restarts (Restart=) since the service was started: a crash loop shows here | | main pid | number | main process id, 0 if not running | | exit status | number | exit status of the last main process | Timers: | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | service | string | the unit the timer starts | | last trigger age | duration | time since the timer last fired; missing if it has not fired | | idle age | duration | time since the timer last fired or, if systemd does not know when it last fired (e.g. after a reboot without Persistent=true), since the timer was activated | | next trigger in | duration | time until the next calendar (OnCalendar=) run; missing if none is scheduled, so always missing for timers with only OnBootSec=/OnActiveSec=/OnUnitActiveSec= | | service result | string | result of the last run of the started unit: success, exit-code, ... | | service exit status | number | exit status of the started service's last main process | | service active state | string | active state of the started unit | Raw: | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | properties | object | {Name: value} for each name in params.properties; integers (sizes, counts, ids) as numbers, everything else as text exactly as systemctl show prints it (infinity, yes, [not set]); a name systemd does not know is missing | duration fields accept unit literals in conditions: idle age: { lt: 25h }. See Checks. Which field to use - Must run: active state: active. Must be stopped: active state: { not equals: active } (a failed unit is not running either). A typo in the unit name makes "must be stopped" pass, because a unit that does not exist is not running: add load state: loaded to rules for units that must be installed. - Starts on boot / must not: unit file state. enabled starts on boot; disabled and masked do not (masked cannot even be started by hand). static units have no [Install] section and are started by something else. - Timer fires regularly: prefer idle age to last trigger age. A timer without Persistent=true forgets when it last fired on every reboot; last trigger age is then missing and a condition on it fails until the timer fires again, up to a whole period after each boot. idle age counts from the timer's activation in that case, and still fails when an active timer has not fired for longer than the threshold. When systemd knows the last run, idle age equals last trigger age, so restarting a timer that stopped firing does not hide it. - The job succeeds: service result: success. Prefer it to service exit status: a unit may declare other exit codes successful (SuccessExitStatus=), and service result already accounts for that. Before the job has run for the first time since boot it is success. - Anything else: name the property in params.properties and check properties.<Name , e.g. properties.MemoryCurrent. Which fields are present: - Service fields only for services, timer fields only for timers. - A unit that does not exist is not an error: systemd reports it with load state: not-found and active state: inactive (and default values such as result: success, restarts: 0 for services). "Must run" then fails with a clear message, "must be stopped" passes. - Older systemd versions do not have some properties (NRestarts appeared in systemd 235); their fields are then missing and conditions on them fail with "got nothing (path is missing)". systemctl missing or failing (e.g. no user service manager for user: true) is an error, not a fail; systemd's message is shown. A rule without check passes whenever the state could be read, as with any module, so always say what you expect. Examples "" in telnet-off covers a unit that is not installed at all. properties.MemoryCurrent is a number (bytes), so lt works on it; it is [not set] when memory accounting is off, and lt then fails with "not applicable to a string". Numbers beyond the int64 range (18446744073709551615, systemd's "unlimited") stay text. A failure names the rule and the value:
title: systemd module

content: Output and results A run reports its outcome in four places: | Where | What | For | |---|---|---| | exit code | did everything pass | cron, systemd, scripts | | stdout | every rule, or only the failing ones; text or JSON | people, pipelines | | <paths.results /<name /<rule .json | the latest result of each rule | dashboards, other tools | | <paths.events / | changes of state | notifications, see State and events | Exit codes | Code | Meaning | |---|---| | 0 | every rule that ran passed (also when there were no rules to run) | | 1 | at least one rule has status fail or error | | 2 | onecheck could not do its job: no or invalid config, unknown flag, another run of the same config in progress, results or events could not be written, the run was interrupted (SIGINT, SIGTERM) | The exit code follows the status of this run , not the confirmed state: a rule with fail after: 3 that failed once already gives 1. With code 2 nothing is printed on stdout; the reason is on stderr, prefixed with onecheck:. An interrupted run (Ctrl-C, systemctl stop, shutdown) kills the running modules together with everything they started and records nothing: no results, no state changes, no events. A half-finished check says nothing about what it was checking, so it must not produce a fail event. Flags | Flag | Effect | |---|---| | -o, --output text\|json | output format, default text | | --only-failed | list only rules with status fail or error; the summary still counts all rules | | --rule <name | run only this rule; repeatable | | --tag <tag | run only rules carrying this tag; repeatable | | --log-level <level | override log.level for this run and also print the log at that level on stderr | With both --rule and --tag, a rule runs if it matches either. Disabled rules (enabled: false) never run. Results are printed on stdout only. Log lines never go to stdout, so onecheck -o json | jq is safe; warnings and errors of onecheck itself go to stderr and to the log file. Text output One line per rule: status, rule name, module and duration. Under a failing rule, one line per condition that did not hold; under an error, the reason. The note in brackets appears when the confirmed state needs explaining: | Note | Meaning | |---|---| | [transition: fail] | this run changed the state to fail; an event was written | | [transition: recovered] | this run changed the state back to pass; an event was written | | [state: pass, 1/3] | the run did not pass, but the state is still pass: 1 of fail after: 3 | | [state: fail, 1/2] | the run passed, but the state is still fail: 1 of pass after: 2 | JSON output summary always counts every rule that ran. results lists them in config order; with --only-failed it contains only the non-passing ones (possibly []). Each element has the result format below. Result files After every run each rule's result is stored at Passing and failing rules alike. There is no history: the file is replaced on each run (atomically, so a reader never sees a half-written file). The directory therefore always shows the current picture of all rules of a config. Results of rules that were removed from the config or disabled are deleted by the next full run (one without --rule / --tag). Result format The same object is used in JSON output, in result files and inside events. | Key | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | config | string | name of the config | | rule | string | rule name | | module | string | module name | | module version | string | version of the module that ran; empty if the module could not be loaded | | tags | array | the rule's tags, [] if none | | status | string | outcome of this run: pass, fail, error | | state | string | confirmed state after this run: pass, fail | | transition | string or null | fail or recovered if this run changed the state, else null | | consecutive | number | how many runs in a row ended like this one (passing, or not passing) | | fail after, pass after | number | the rule's thresholds | | started at | string | start of the check, UTC, RFC 3339 | | duration ms | number | how long the check took | | failures | array | conditions that did not hold; [] unless status is fail | | error | string or null | why the check could not run; set only when status is error | | output | object | what the module saw, kept for diagnosis; {} if the module has no output fields or output tail is 0. See Saved output | Each element of failures: | Key | Description | |---|---| | path | the key of check the condition belongs to, e.g. body, headers.content-type | | json path | location inside a parsed JSON document, for json.assert (GJSON path) and json.schema (JSON pointer); absent otherwise | | operator | the operator that did not hold, e.g. equals, length gt, any, not, json, schema | | expected | the operator's argument from the config | | actual | the value found; null if the path was missing; long values are cut to about 1 KB | | message | a ready-to-show sentence combining the above | Saved output A failed exit code: 0 alone does not say what went wrong. So onecheck keeps the raw output of the check in the result, whether or not a condition uses it and whether the rule passed or failed : | Module | Saved fields | |---|---| | command | stdout, stderr | | http | body, headers | | file | nothing | Which fields are saved is decided by the module (it marks them as output, see Module protocol); how much is kept is decided by the config: - The size is per field and accepts k, m (1k, 10k, 1m) as well as KB, MB; a bare number is bytes. - A longer text is cut to its last output tail bytes and then starts with …: the end of the output is where the error usually is. - A value that is not text (headers) is kept whole if it fits into output tail and left out otherwise. - A command killed by its timeout still has the output it printed before that in output, next to status: error. - Output is cut from what the module returned, which is itself limited by run.max field size (default 10MB): of a larger output only the first max field size bytes are seen at all. The result file is overwritten by the next run, so output always belongs to the latest run. An event embeds the result of the run that changed the state, including its output, so a notification can show why the check failed. Saved output may contain secrets (tokens in a response body, passwords printed by a script). Result directories are created with mode 0750 and files with 0640; set output tail: 0 on rules whose output must not be stored.
title: Output and results

content: State and events onecheck does not only tell whether a check passes right now. For every rule it keeps a confirmed state between runs and records each change of that state as an event . This is what a notification service builds on: it gets told when something broke and when it recovered, once per change, regardless of which module the rule uses. Status and state Two different things are reported for each rule: | | Values | Meaning | |---|---|---| | status | pass, fail, error | the outcome of this run | | state | pass, fail | the confirmed state, which changes only after enough runs in a row | status values: - pass — every condition held; - fail — at least one condition did not hold; - error — the check could not be carried out: module missing or incompatible, invalid rule, timeout, no connection, value too large. For the state, error counts the same as fail: a check that cannot run is not known to be healthy. The distinction stays visible in status. Thresholds: fail after, pass after Both default to 1 (from defaults in the config), which means the state follows the status immediately. The rules: - In state pass, after fail after consecutive runs that did not pass, the state becomes fail. - In state fail, after pass after consecutive passing runs, the state becomes pass. - A run with the opposite outcome resets the count. - A rule seen for the first time starts in state pass without an event. If it is failing, it goes to fail through the normal fail after rule. Example with fail after: 3, pass after: 2: | Run | status | consecutive | state | event | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | pass | 1 | pass | | | 2 | fail | 1 | pass | | | 3 | fail | 2 | pass | | | 4 | pass | 1 | pass | (count reset) | | 5 | fail | 1 | pass | | | 6 | fail | 2 | pass | | | 7 | fail | 3 | fail | fail | | 8 | fail | 4 | fail | | | 9 | pass | 1 | fail | | | 10 | pass | 2 | pass | recovered | Thresholds count runs , not time: with a cron line every minute, fail after: 3 means roughly three minutes. The process exit code and the printed output follow status, not state: a rule that failed once with fail after: 3 already makes onecheck exit with 1. The text output shows the gap, e.g. [state: pass, 1/3]. A manual onecheck run --rule <name updates the state and writes events exactly like a scheduled run. Events Every change of a rule's confirmed state writes one file into the event queue directory, paths.events: The file name is the event id: <UTC time -<config name -<rule -<transition . | Key | Description | |---|---| | id | unique id, equal to the file name without .json | | config | name of the config the rule belongs to | | rule | rule name | | transition | fail (pass → fail) or recovered (fail → pass) | | from, to | confirmed state before and after | | at | when the change was recorded (UTC, RFC 3339) | | expires at | at + events.ttl; after this the event may be deleted | | result | the full result of the run that caused the change, see Output and results | For a recovered event, result is the passing run (failures is empty). For a fail event caused by a check that could not run, result.status is error and result.error holds the reason. Consuming the queue The queue is a plain directory, shared by all configs on the host. The contract for a consumer (the notification service): 1. List .json files. Files are written atomically (temp file + rename), so a visible .json file is always complete. Ignore names starting with .. 2. Process the event. 3. Delete the file. Ordering: file names start with a UTC timestamp, so a lexicographic sort is chronological. Delivery is at-least-once: if a consumer crashes between processing and deleting, it will see the event again. Use id to deduplicate. Events nobody consumed are removed by onecheck logrotate once expires at has passed (events.ttl, default 24h). See Logging and logrotate. No lost transitions For each rule onecheck writes the event first and the new state after it. If the event cannot be written (disk full, no permission), the state is left unchanged and the run ends with exit code 2; the next run detects the same change again and retries. A change of state is therefore either in the queue or reported as a failed run, never silently dropped. Files | Path | Content | Lifetime | |---|---|---| | <paths.state /<name /<rule .json | confirmed state and consecutive counters | internal, do not edit | | <paths.state /<name /.lock, .owner | run lock; which config file owns the name | internal | | <paths.results /<name /<rule .json | latest result of the rule | overwritten every run | | <paths.events /<id .json | one state change | until consumed or expired | State and result files of a rule that was removed from the config (or disabled) are deleted by the next full run, that is a run without --rule or --tag. A state file that cannot be read is logged as a warning and the rule is treated as new. Renaming a rule starts it from scratch: the state is keyed by rule name. Changing a rule's module or conditions keeps its state.
title: State and events
